dialogs.title: संवाद — The family photo on the wall
dialogs.intro: Priya shows Ani a photo of her big family. In line seven Priya praises Ani's Hindi — notice the word she uses, and why it isn't the one you might expect.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: This is a photo of our family.
lines.literal: this — our — family — of(fem.) — picture — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: wow! this(polite) — your — father — ji — is?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Yes, and this is my mother.
lines.literal: ji — yes, and — this(polite) — my(fem.) — mother — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: and — this — small — boy — who — is?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.literal: that — my — brother — of(masc.) — son — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Thank you. Whose house is this?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:

lines.literal: this — my — grandfather — ji — of(masc.) — house — is, Lucknow — in.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: It's beautiful. My grandfather's house is old too.

lines.literal: five — mom, dad, two — brothers, and — I.

notes: **The heart of this unit: का, की, and के agree with the gender of the thing OWNED — the owner makes no difference at all.** *राम **की** किताब* = "Ram's book", and it's की because **किताब is feminine**, not because Ram is a woman. *प्रिया **का** घर* = "Priya's house", का because **घर is masculine**, not because Priya is a man. ⚠️ English *his/her* looks at the owner, so your instinct will keep telling you to do the same. Don't. Look at the thing.

**आपकी हिंदी अच्छी है — feminine twice, because हिंदी is feminine.** Compare *आपका घर अच्छा है* (your house is nice) — masculine twice, because घर is masculine. Possessive and adjective walk together, both following the same noun.

**के shows up in two different situations.** First, when the thing is masculine plural: *मेरे भाई* (my brothers). Second, and more often, when **a postposition follows the noun**: *आप**के** परिवार **में*** — परिवार is singular and masculine, but because में comes after it, आपका becomes आपके. This is the **oblique form**, covered fully in unit 7. For now, learn the pattern: postposition after → use के.

**पिता जी हैं, not है — and माँ takes हैं too.** Parents and older people always take the plural as a sign of respect, just like आप. That's why Priya says *ये मेरी माँ **हैं***, not *है*. ⚠️ Using the singular for your parents sounds rude to Indian ears, however "logical" the grammar.

**किसका, किसकी, किसके = "whose", and it too follows the thing.** *यह **किसका** घर है?* (whose house is this?) but *यह **किसकी** किताब है?* (whose book is this?). The answer can be just the owner: *प्रिया का* — "Priya's".

**Hindi kinship words are far more precise than English ones, and the difference matters.** English has one word, "uncle", for all of them; Hindi distinguishes **चाचा** (father's younger brother), **ताऊ** (father's elder brother), **मामा** (mother's brother), and **फूफा** (husband of father's sister). Grandfathers too: **दादा** on the father's side, **नाना** on the mother's. ⚠️ This isn't fussiness; in an Indian family the relationship decides who is respected how. When in doubt, **अंकल जी** and **आंटी जी** are safe for anyone.

**पापा and मम्मी are widely used and not considered Westernized at all.** In everyday speech Indians say *पापा* more often than *पिता जी* — the latter sounds rather formal, like "Father". To sound natural, say **पापा** and **मम्मी** for your own parents, and **पिता जी** / **माता जी** when talking about someone else's.

grammars.title: Possessives: one table for life
body: Which column you use is decided by the thing to its right, not the owner to its left.

head: Owner
+ masculine thing
+ masculine plural, or before a postposition
+ feminine thing

after: ⚠️ Look at the last row: with names or ordinary nouns, the possessive stands **separately** as का/की/के after the name — like English *'s*. *प्रिया की बहन* = "Priya's sister". *मेरे भाई का बेटा* = "my brother's son" — note **मेरे** (because भाई is followed by का), then **का** (because बेटा is masculine). Two decisions in a row, and both look to the right.

sections.title: The extended family, and the questions that always come

blocks.text: Family is the first topic Indians open with strangers — often before work, almost always before politics. These four questions will come, and having your answers ready makes your first conversations far more enjoyable.

head: Question
Pronunciation
Sample answer
rows: आपके परिवार में कितने लोग हैं?
aap-ke pa-ri-vaar meⁿ kit-ne log haiⁿ
क्या आप बड़े हैं या छोटे?
kyaa aap ba-Re haiⁿ yaa chho-Te
आपके घर में कौन कौन है?
aap-ke ghar meⁿ kaun kaun hai

blocks.title: Three things that make your answers sound natural
items: **कौन कौन है** — a repeated question word means "who all", not just "who". Likewise *क्या क्या* (what all) and *कहाँ कहाँ* (where all). This doubling is very typical of Hindi — it's where Indian English gets its "who all are coming?".
**हम पाँच लोग हैं** — "we're five people", not "there are five people in my family". The shorter version is the one that sounds native.
**सबसे छोटी** — "the youngest". सबसे literally means "than all", and it's how Hindi forms superlatives. Unit 18 covers it.

blocks.text: A note that may warm your heart. In Indian families the word **जी** you learned in unit 1 is used with parents all day long — *पापा जी*, *दादी जी* — and many adults still touch their parents' feet as a greeting on special days. If you go home with an Indian friend, nobody expects you to do that; a **नमस्ते** with palms together, a slight bow, and a **जी** are more than enough, and they'll be remembered.
